name: Borno
summary_text: Borno is one of the twelve northern states applying Sharia criminal law in parallel with the federal system since the 1999-2002 wave. The Sharia Penal Code criminalises same-sex acts between men and women for Muslims, with penalties reaching beyond the federal 14-year SSMPA term. No trans-specific incident, Hisbah activity, or USCIRF case documentation is on record for Borno in this dossier. The legal framework itself is the finding; absence of documented enforcement is a reporting-decay limitation (TIERs states its figures represent 'only a fraction of the true scale'), not evidence of safety. Score 0.024 below the national 0.08. Same justification as the seven-state generic-Sharia bloc (Borno, Gombe, Jigawa, Kaduna, Katsina, Kebbi, Niger): enacted capital-capable criminal law adding a parallel court jurisdiction, but without the documented Hisbah enforcement layer or case-level evidence that pulls Yobe (0.04), Zamfara (0.05), Kano/Sokoto (0.03), or Bauchi (0.02) lower.

sources.claim_summary: Human Rights Watch report (2004) on the extension of Sharia to criminal law in Nigeria: Zamfara's governor was first, introducing the Sharia Establishment Law on 27 October 1999 (in force 27 January 2000), and by 2002 twelve northern states had adopted some form of Sharia into their criminal legislation - to date the only states where Sharia courts have jurisdiction to try criminal cases.

UK Home Office country-of-origin information note (June 2025) on sexual orientation and gender identity in Nigeria: Islamic law applies to Muslims in the 12 northern states and criminalises same-sex sexual acts both between men and between women; the maximum penalty for 'sodomy' for men is death in all 12 states and penalties for 'lesbianism' range from death to flogging and imprisonment; includes a dedicated section on enforcement of Sharia provisions and the attitude of the hisbah (morality police).
